title: The Way of Action
intro: 88 days through chapters 3 to 6 of the Bhagavad Gita: action, knowledge, renunciation and meditation.

posts.caption: This plan walks through chapters 3 to 6. One traditional reading groups 1 to 6 as the Gita's section on action (karma), before devotion (bhakti) in 7 to 12 and knowledge (jnana) in 13 to 18. In chapter 2 Krishna ranked buddhi, steady understanding (Besant's "knowledge"), above mere action. So Arjuna asks: then why urge him into this terrible battle? Janardana and Keshava are names of Krishna.

Arjuna presses on: Krishna's words seem mixed, praising steady understanding yet urging him to act, and they leave him confused. He asks for the one sure way to the highest good (shreyas, Besant's "bliss"). Much of the Gita moves like this, with Arjuna asking honest questions and Krishna answering at length.

Krishna answers that there are two paths, as he has taught before: jnana yoga, the discipline of knowledge, followed by the Sankhyas, and karma yoga, the discipline of action, followed by the yogis. Sankhya here means the path of discernment, though the word is also the name of one of the classical schools of Indian philosophy.

Freedom from the bonds of action (naishkarmya, literally "actionlessness") is not won by simply not starting anything, Krishna says, nor by renunciation (sannyasa) alone. This sets up the chapter's main claim: the way out of action's bonds runs through action done rightly, not through stopping.

No one can stay actionless even for a moment, Krishna says. Everyone is driven by the gunas, the three qualities of nature (prakriti): sattva (clarity), rajas (activity and passion) and tamas (inertia). Because body and mind are always moving under their influence, giving up action entirely is not really possible.

Krishna describes a person who holds the body still but keeps dwelling on sense objects in the mind. Besant's "hypocrite" translates mithyachara, literally "one whose conduct is false." Outer stillness without inner restraint, the verse suggests, is only a show of renunciation.

"Right action" translates niyatam karma, which commentators read as prescribed or necessary action, one's regular duties. Krishna adds a practical point: without acting, even keeping the body going would be impossible. The Sanskrit phrase is sharira-yatra, literally "the body's journey."

Yajna, sacrifice, originally meant the Vedic fire ritual. Krishna widens it: action done as an offering, without attachment, does not bind, while action done only for oneself keeps the world "bound by action." Shankara, among other commentators, reads yajna here as the Lord himself, citing the Vedic saying "sacrifice is Vishnu."

Those who eat what remains after the sacrifice are freed from wrongdoing; those who cook only for themselves "eat sin." The verse is often linked with prasada, food first offered to the divine and then shared, a practice found in many Hindu homes and temples.

Krishna sketches a cycle: living beings come from food, food from rain, rain from sacrifice, and sacrifice from action. Two verses later he calls it a turning wheel that each person is meant to keep moving. Human action, in this picture, is part of how the whole world is sustained.

posts.display: But the man who rejoiceth in the Self, with the Self is satisfied, and is content in the Self, for him verily there is nothing to do.
posts.caption: After stressing duty, Krishna names an exception: one who delights only in the Self (atman), satisfied and content within, has nothing left that must be done. Shankara reads this as the realized knower, for whom action has fallen away. Even so, Krishna goes straight on to urge Arjuna to act.

Krishna draws his conclusion: Arjuna is to do the work that is his, steadily and without attachment, since unattached action leads to the Supreme. This is the core of karma yoga, the discipline of action, and the chapter's key instruction.

Krishna offers an example: Janaka, the king of Videha who appears in the Upanishads as a wise royal sage, reached perfection through action while still ruling. Besant's "welfare of the world" translates lokasangraha, literally "holding the world together," an idea Krishna returns to a few verses later.

Krishna adds a social reason to act: people follow the example of those they look up to, and the standard such a person sets is the one others live by. Arjuna, a famous warrior and prince, is one of those people. In the verses that follow, Krishna points to his own example.

Krishna points to himself: there is nothing in the three worlds he must do or gain, and yet he keeps acting. The three worlds are traditionally earth, the space between, and heaven. It is an early hint of the divine identity Krishna reveals more fully later in the Gita.

The unwise act out of attachment; the wise act just as fully, but without it, for lokasangraha, "holding the world together," its welfare and order. Modern readers like Tilak and Gandhi, both deeply engaged in public life, put this ideal of selfless action at the center of their readings of the Gita.

Krishna asks the wise not to unsettle those still attached to their work. The Sanskrit buddhi-bheda means "splitting the understanding." Instead, acting wholeheartedly themselves, the wise make all action attractive. It continues the chapter's theme of leading by example.

All actions are carried out by the gunas, the three qualities of nature (prakriti), Krishna says, yet the self, deluded by ahankara, the ego (literally "I-maker"), thinks "I am the doer." The wise, he adds next, see only "the gunas moving among the gunas," and so stay unattached.

Krishna ties action to devotion: all actions are to be surrendered to him, with the mind on the Self, free of craving and the sense of "mine," and the battle fought with the "fever" (jvara) gone. Commentators across schools read this as action offered to the divine, which no longer binds.

Even the wise act according to their own nature (prakriti), Krishna says; all beings follow their nature, so what can mere suppression achieve? Commentators read this not as dismissing self-control, which the next verse urges, but as a warning that forcing against one's nature fails.

Raga and dvesha, attraction and aversion, sit in each sense's relation to its objects. Krishna calls them "obstructors of the path," paripanthin, a word that can mean a robber waiting by the road. Patanjali's Yoga Sutras also list this pair among the kleshas, the afflictions of the mind.

One of the Gita's best-known lines: better one's own dharma (svadharma), even done imperfectly, than another's done well. In context, Arjuna, a warrior, is tempted to leave the battle for a renunciant's life. Traditional commentators link svadharma to the duties of one's varna, or social class, and stage of life; many modern readers take it as one's own nature and calling.

Arjuna asks a very human question: what drives a person to do wrong, unwillingly, as if forced? Krishna's answer, desire (kama) and the anger that comes from it, fills the rest of chapter 3. Varshneya, "descendant of Vrishni," names Krishna by his clan.

Chapter 4 opens with Krishna tracing this yoga back to Vivasvan, the sun god, and down a line of royal sages, until over time it was lost. He teaches it again now because Arjuna is his devotee (bhakta) and his friend (sakha). In the Mahabharata they are cousins and close companions, and Krishna is serving as Arjuna's charioteer.

Arjuna has asked how Krishna, born so recently, could have taught this yoga to the ancient sun god. Krishna's reply: both of them have passed through many births, but only Krishna remembers his. The verses that follow explain why the divine is born "from age to age," the teaching later known as avatara, "descent." Parantapa, "scorcher of foes," is Arjuna.

Many people, freed from passion, fear and anger, absorbed in Krishna and taking refuge in him, purified by the "austerity of knowledge" (jnana-tapas), have reached his own state of being. Schools differ on what that means: oneness with the divine for Advaita, or sharing the divine's nature for Vishishtadvaita and others.

One of the Gita's most quoted verses: however people approach Krishna, he receives them, for all paths are his. Vivekananda quoted it in his famous 1893 address in Chicago to illustrate the acceptance of all faiths. Classical commentators like Shankara often read it more narrowly, as the Lord answering each according to how they seek him.

Actions do not stain Krishna, and he has no longing for their results. Whoever understands this about him is not bound by action either. Besant's "affect" translates a word that literally means "smear" or "stain," a picture that returns with the lotus leaf in chapter 5.

The seekers of liberation (mumukshu) of old, Krishna says, knew this and still acted, so Arjuna should act as they did. "This" is the previous verse's teaching: just as actions do not stain the divine, they need not bind one who acts without craving their fruit.

Even the wise are confused about what action and inaction really are, Krishna says, using the word kavi, which means both poet and seer. He promises to explain the kind of action that frees from the inauspicious (ashubha). The verses that follow are some of the most paradoxical in the Gita.

Krishna names three things to understand: karma (action), vikarma (usually read as wrong or forbidden action, Besant's "unlawful action") and akarma (inaction). "Mysterious" translates gahana, which also means deep or dense, like a thick forest: the way of action is hard to see through.

The central paradox of chapter 4: seeing inaction in action and action in inaction. One common reading: the wise act fully yet are inwardly free of "I am the doer," while someone sitting still may still be acting in the mind. Shankara reads it as the knower seeing the Self as actionless even while the body acts.

The wise call someone a pandita, a sage, whose undertakings are free of desire-driven intention (kama-sankalpa) and whose actions are burned in the "fire of knowledge" (jnanagni). Fire runs through this chapter, borrowed from the Vedic sacrifice and turned inward.

Having let go of attachment to results, always content, depending on nothing, such a person "does nothing at all," even while busy with action. "Nowhere seeking refuge" (nirashraya) is read as not leaning on outside things for security. It is the paradox of inaction in action, now drawn as a portrait.

Content with whatever comes unsought, beyond the "pairs of opposites" like heat and cold or praise and blame, free of envy, and steady in success and failure, the sage acts and is not bound. The Gita repeatedly pictures freedom as this kind of balance.

Recited as a grace before meals in many Hindu homes and schools. Every part of the offering, the ghee, the fire, the one who offers and the act of offering, is Brahman, the ultimate reality (Besant's "the Eternal"). Advaita reads it as all being one Brahman; other schools, as everything belonging to and pervaded by the divine.

Krishna has been listing kinds of sacrifice: offerings of wealth, austerity, study and the breath (pranayama), among others. All are "born of action," he says, and knowing this brings freedom. "Before the Eternal" renders brahmano mukhe, literally "in the mouth of Brahman," which Shankara reads as "in the Vedas."

After listing many kinds of sacrifice, Krishna ranks them: the sacrifice of knowledge (jnana-yajna) is better than any offering of material things, and all action finds its completion in knowledge. From here, chapter 4 turns toward knowledge, the theme of its closing verses.

Even the worst wrongdoer can cross all wrongdoing on the "raft of knowledge" (jnana-plava). Crossing a river or sea to the far shore is an old image of liberation across Indian traditions: Jains call their great teachers tirthankaras, "ford-makers," and the Buddha compared his teaching to a raft.

Nothing in this world purifies like knowledge, Krishna says. The word for "purifier," pavitra, is often used of holy rivers, places and rites; here it describes understanding. The one perfected in yoga finds this knowledge within, in time.

Often quoted in Sanskrit on its own: the person of faith (shraddha) gains knowledge. Krishna pairs faith with devotion to the goal and mastery of the senses, and says knowledge leads quickly to supreme peace (shanti).

The other side of the previous verse, which promised knowledge and peace to the person of faith: the ignorant, faithless "doubting self" (samshayatma) comes to ruin, with happiness neither here nor beyond. Arjuna's crisis began in doubt, which may be why Krishna dwells on it as chapter 4 closes.

Chapter 4 ends with a call: cut the doubt in the heart with the sword of knowledge, take up yoga, and stand up (uttishtha). It echoes chapter 2, where Krishna first told Arjuna to rise. Bharata, "descendant of Bharata," is one of Arjuna's family names.

Chapter 5 opens with Arjuna puzzled again. Krishna has praised sannyasa, the renunciation of action, and also karma yoga, disciplined action, so Arjuna asks plainly which one is better. The whole chapter is Krishna's answer, and it suggests the two are less opposed than they look.

Krishna's answer: renunciation and karma yoga both lead to the highest good, but karma yoga is the better of the two. Shankara, who championed formal renunciation, reads this as advice for those not yet established in knowledge. Ramanuja takes it more generally, holding that karma yoga is the easier and surer path.

Krishna redefines the renunciate. The true sannyasi, "always a renouncer" (nitya-sannyasi), is marked not by giving up home or work but by an inner state: neither hating nor craving. Free of the pairs of opposites, such a person is released from bondage with ease.

Krishna has just said that only the childish call the paths of knowledge (Sankhya) and action (Yoga) different. Here he adds that renunciation (sannyasa) is hard to reach without yoga, while a sage steadied by yoga soon reaches Brahman, "the Eternal." Besant keeps the Sanskrit muni, sage; the related word mauna means silence.

A portrait of the yogi: purified, self-mastered, senses controlled, the self become "the Self of all beings." Such a person acts and is not tainted. Advaita reads the phrase as realizing one Self in all; Ramanuja, as seeing every self as alike in its essential nature.

The harmonized knower thinks "I do nothing at all," even while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping and breathing. The list runs on into the next verse. Behind it is the idea from chapter 3 that nature's qualities (gunas) do the acting, and only the self deluded by ego thinks "I am the doer."

A famous image: one who acts without attachment, placing all actions in Brahman, is untouched by wrongdoing, as a lotus leaf is by water. Lotus leaves really do shed water, which beads up and rolls off. Rooted in mud yet unstained, the lotus is one of India's oldest symbols of purity.

The yukta, the person "yoked" or harmonized, lets go of the fruit of action and reaches lasting peace. The ayukta, "unyoked," driven by desire and clinging to results, is bound. Both words come from the root yuj, to yoke or join, the same root as yoga.

The "nine-gated city" is the body, with its nine openings: two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, the mouth, and the two lower openings. The embodied self lives in it at ease, like a sovereign, neither acting nor making others act. The Shvetashvatara Upanishad also speaks of the body as a city of nine gates.

The all-pervading Lord (vibhu) takes on no one's wrong or good deeds, Krishna says. Beings are confused because knowledge is covered over by ignorance (ajnana). The next verse continues the image, with knowledge shining like the sun once ignorance is gone.

Those wholly given to "That," in thought, in self, in steadiness and in devotion, reach the state from which there is no return: freedom from the cycle of rebirth (samsara). "That" (tat) is usually read as the ultimate reality, Brahman or God, as in the Chandogya Upanishad's famous teaching tat tvam asi, "you are That," though Ramanuja takes it here as the individual self in its pure state.

The wise see with an equal eye a learned, humble Brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and an outcaste (shvapaka, literally "dog-cooker," a term for people pushed to the margins of the society of the time). Commentators read it as seeing the same Self, or selves of the same nature, in all. Some modern readers cite it against caste prejudice.

The knower of Brahman, firm in understanding and free of delusion, neither rejoices at getting what is pleasant nor is shaken by what is unpleasant. The portrait echoes the sthita-prajna, the person of steady wisdom, described at the end of chapter 2.

Pleasures born of contact between the senses and their objects are "wombs of pain" (duhkha-yoni), Krishna says, because they have a beginning and an end. The wise do not rest their joy there. Kaunteya, "son of Kunti," is one of Arjuna's names.

Whoever can withstand the surge (vega) of desire and anger (krodha, Besant's "passion") here in this life, before leaving the body, is the harmonized and happy person. Vega suggests a rush, like a current or a flood. The Gita treats desire and anger as forces to be withstood, not denied.

Happy within, delighting within, lit from within: such a yogi, becoming Brahman, reaches brahma-nirvana. Nirvana, "blowing out" like a flame, is best known from Buddhism; the Gita pairs it with Brahman, as it did at the end of chapter 2, for a peace found in the ultimate reality.

Rishis, seers whose impurities are gone and whose doubts are cut, self-controlled and devoted to the welfare of all beings, reach the peace of Brahman. That phrase, rejoicing in the good of all beings (sarva-bhuta-hite ratah), returns in chapter 12 to describe those who come to Krishna.

Chapter 5 closes with Krishna naming himself: enjoyer of every sacrifice and austerity, great lord of all worlds, and friend (suhrid) of all beings. Besant renders suhrid as "Lover," a friend who wishes one well. Knowing him this way, one comes to peace.

Chapter 6 turns to meditation (dhyana), but first redefines renunciation. The true sannyasi and yogi is one who does the work to be done without depending on its fruit, not one who simply gives up the sacred fire and rites. Abandoning the household fire was a traditional mark of a formal renunciant.

For the sage who wants to climb (arurukshu) to yoga, action is the means; for the one who has climbed (yogarudha), calm (shama) is the means. The word arudha means "mounted," as on a horse or a height. Many commentators read this as stages on one path.

Krishna describes the yogi who is "harmonised" (yukta): content in knowledge, steady, senses mastered, seeing a lump of earth, a stone and gold as the same. Commentators often distinguish jnana, knowledge gained from teaching, from vijnana, knowledge made one's own through experience.

Krishna lists the people one meets in life, from well-wishers, friends and relatives to the indifferent, the hostile, and even the good and the wicked. The one who regards them all with an even mind (sama-buddhi) excels. Equanimity, in the Gita, applies to people as much as to circumstances.

Now the meditation instructions begin. The yogi practices constantly, alone, in a secluded place, mind and body controlled, without longing or possessiveness. "Free from greed" translates aparigraha, non-grasping, also one of the five yamas, the ethical restraints, in Patanjali's Yoga Sutras.

posts.display: Holding the body, head and neck erect, immovably steady, looking fixedly at the point of the nose, with unseeing gaze.
posts.caption: Body, head and neck held straight and still, gaze resting on the tip of the nose, not looking around. Shankara explains it as gazing "as if" at the nose, a way to keep the eyes from wandering, not a literal stare. Similar posture instructions appear in the Shvetashvatara Upanishad.

Krishna sums up the meditation instructions: the yogi who keeps the mind controlled and constantly turned toward the Self comes to peace. The Sanskrit calls it a peace "culminating in nirvana" (nirvana-paramam), Besant's "supreme Bliss." It "abideth in Me," Krishna says, linking meditation with devotion to him.

Yoga is not for one who eats too much or too little, or sleeps too much or too little. The Gita's method is moderation rather than extreme austerity. Some readers compare it to the Buddha's middle way between indulgence and self-mortification.

For one balanced in eating and recreation, in effort at work, and in sleep and waking, yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrow (duhkha-ha). The word yukta, "balanced" or "regulated," comes three times in the Sanskrit, setting the rhythm of a well-ordered life.

One of the Gita's best-loved images: the disciplined mind of the yogi absorbed in meditation is like a lamp in a windless place, whose flame does not flicker. The picture is not of a flame put out, but of one burning steadily, awake and still.

A famous definition: yoga is the "disconnection from union with pain" (duhkha-samyoga-viyoga). It plays on the word yoga, which means union or yoking, by defining it as a separation. Krishna adds that it is to be practiced with resolve and an undiscouraged heart.

Little by little (shanaih shanaih, "slowly, slowly"), with the understanding held firm, the mind settles in the Self and thinks of nothing else. The doubled word stresses that meditation is gradual, not forced. "Gain tranquillity" translates uparamet, "let him come to rest."

Whenever the restless, unsteady mind wanders off, it is brought back under the Self's control, as often as it strays. The instruction is simple: notice the wandering, return. That same basic movement is at the heart of many meditation methods practiced today.

Supreme happiness comes to the yogi whose mind is at peace, Krishna says. Besant's "passion-nature" is rajas, the restless guna, here stilled, and "of the nature of the Eternal" translates brahma-bhuta, "become Brahman." Advaita reads that as oneness with Brahman; other schools, as gaining a pure nature like Brahman's.

The yogi sees the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self, seeing the same everywhere. The Isha Upanishad has a closely similar line. Advaita reads this as one Self in all; Ramanuja, as seeing all selves as alike in their nature.

Now Krishna speaks of himself: whoever sees him everywhere and everything in him, he never loses, and that person never loses him. The vision of the Self in all, from the previous verse, becomes a personal bond with the divine, a theme the next six chapters develop.

Whoever, "established in unity," worships Krishna as dwelling in all beings lives in him, Krishna says, "whatever his mode of living." That closing phrase suggests such a yogi abides in the divine whatever his outward life. Here the vision of oneness and devotion (bhakti) meet.

Through atmaupamya, "likeness to oneself," the perfect yogi sees the same in all, in pleasure or in pain. Shankara reads it as feeling others' joy and suffering as one's own, and draws from it a principle of non-harm (ahimsa). Many readers see in it a Gita version of the golden rule.

Arjuna objects: the mind is restless, turbulent, strong and stubborn, as hard to hold back as the wind. It is one of the most relatable lines in the Gita, and Krishna does not brush it aside. His reply comes in the next verse.

Krishna agrees the mind is hard to control, but says it can be held by abhyasa, steady practice, and vairagya, dispassion or non-attachment. Patanjali's Yoga Sutras (1.12) name the same pair as the way to still the mind.

Krishna adds that yoga is hard to reach for one whose self is uncontrolled, but the self-controlled can reach it by striving through the right means (upaya). Besant's "methinks" renders iti me matih, "this is my view." With the previous verse, it frames stilling the mind as a skill built by steady, well-directed effort.

Arjuna asks about a person who has faith and tries, but whose mind slips from yoga before reaching perfection. What becomes of them? It is a question for anyone who starts a spiritual practice and falls short.

Krishna's reassurance: neither here nor hereafter is such a person lost, for no one who does good comes to a bad end. "O beloved" translates tata, a tender word used between father and son or for a dear younger person, found only here in the Gita.

posts.display: Having attained to the worlds of the pure-doing, and having dwelt there for immemorial years, he who fell from yoga is reborn in a pure and blessed house.
posts.caption: What becomes of one who falls short in yoga (yoga-bhrashta): after long years in the worlds of the virtuous, such a person is reborn into a pure and fortunate family. It echoes Krishna's promise in chapter 2 that no effort on this path is ever lost.

The yogi who keeps striving, purified and perfected through many births (aneka-janma), reaches the highest goal. Krishna pictures spiritual growth as a long journey, sometimes across lifetimes, rather than a single leap.

The yogi is greater than ascetics (tapasvi), greater than the learned (jnani), greater than the doers of ritual action (karmi), so Krishna urges Arjuna to become a yogi. Shankara reads jnani here as those learned in scripture, not the realized knower the Gita praises elsewhere.

The last verse of chapter 6, and of this plan: of all yogis, the one who worships Krishna with faith, the inner self absorbed in him, is the most united (yuktatama). It points ahead to bhakti, devotion, the theme of the chapters that follow. Thank you for walking the way of action together.
